name: Ethnocacerism
summary: Ethnocacerism is a Peruvian Indigenous ethnonationalism devised by Isaac Humala and carried into action by his sons Ollanta and Antauro, named after the war hero Andres Avelino Caceres. It presents the 'copper race' of Andean Peruvians as the rightful core of the nation, seeks historical revenge on the white and criollo elite, and looks back to the Inca state as a model. In practice it combines military-led insurrection, hostility to Chile, a state-led protectionist economy and socially conservative, machista positions, and critics describe it as having fascist traits.
scope: The radical etnocacerista movement as formulated by Isaac Humala and led by Antauro Humala (Locumba 2000, Andahuaylazo 2005, the ASPRET reservists and the Antauro-led parties). It excludes the moderated 'integrative nationalism' of Ollanta Humala's Partido Nacionalista Peruano and his 2011-2016 government. Primary voices are Isaac and Antauro Humala in interviews; the movement's own Ideario text could not be opened, so many answers are inferred.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: Antauro Humala's party would subordinate the free market to national production and nationalise foreign firms, so adherents reject market primacy.

public-ownership.rationale: The party programme reported by Panamericana calls for taking foreign companies into state hands, which covers energy and other strategic industries.

property-fundamental.rationale: The programme includes nationalising foreign companies and expropriating media outlets, so private property yields to national interest.

worker-ownership.rationale: Economic proposals are state nationalisation, not collective worker ownership; the movement frames class as secondary to race and nation.

strong-leader.rationale: Led by a military caudillo-style figure; Antauro Humala has argued Peru's dictatorships were more peaceful than its democracies.

state-harmful.rationale: The programme relies on a powerful state that nationalises industry and takes over media, the opposite of abolishing the state.

empower-police-military.rationale: The movement was born inside the army and runs on reservist militia; adherents want a strong, politically central military.

same-sex-marriage.rationale: Antauro Humala calls homosexuality an aberration and a monstrosity and says civil unions are stupid and he is totally against them.

correct-racial-injustice.rationale: CIDOB describes the doctrine as historical revenge for the copper race, aiming to reverse centuries of white-dominated rule.

gender-social-construct.rationale: Critics document machista views on women and hostility to homosexuality, which treat gender roles as natural.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: The doctrine is rooted in Peru's historical Indigenous civilizations and treats cultural continuity as its core.

gradual-change.rationale: The movement staged the Locumba revolt and the Andahuaylazo and calls to refound the republic, rejecting incremental change.

free-trade.rationale: Programme would put domestic production ahead of imports and subordinate the free market.

nation-first.rationale: Isaac Humala says Peru needs a war to wake up and demands territory back, treating national interest as paramount.

open-borders.rationale: Antauro calls current borders colonial impositions but wants Andean unification under a nationalist state, not worldwide open borders.

revolution-justified.rationale: The Humala brothers led armed uprisings at Locumba (2000) and Andahuaylas (2005) to overthrow sitting governments.

central-planning.rationale: The programme prioritises national production over imports and nationalisation, close to planning though no explicit planned economy is documented.

socialized-markets.rationale: Neither a state-socialist nor market-socialist model is spelled out; the movement is split between nationalist market and statist leanings.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: Priority for domestic production over imports is a stated plank of the Antauro Humala party.

one-party-rule.rationale: Analysts cite fascist-like features, and its leader is dismissive of liberal democracy; no explicit one-party programme found.

democracy-best.rationale: Antauro Humala argues Peru's dictatorships have been more peaceful than its democracies, and the movement tried to topple elected governments.

right-to-secede.rationale: The movement wants unification of an Andean homeland and treats existing borders as artificial; it would not favour regions leaving Peru.

natural-rulers.rationale: CIDOB reports the doctrine asserts the supremacy of the copper race, implying a natural fitness to lead, though sources are secondhand.

political-violence-never.rationale: Adherents staged armed uprisings; the Andahuaylazo siege left several people dead.

war-builds-character.rationale: Isaac Humala says explicitly that Peru needs a war with Chile to wake up.

private-courts-defense.rationale: Statism and nationalisation of key industries rule out privatised policing and defence.

military-superiority.rationale: Isaac Humala's talk of war and recovering lost territory presupposes military strength.

ethnic-nation.rationale: The doctrine is explicitly ethnonationalist, centring the copper race as the nation.

class-struggle-history.rationale: The movement frames history as racial revenge rather than class conflict, and rejects the Eurocentric left.

indigenous-land-authority.rationale: Based in Indigenous communities and aims at Indigenous political primacy over a recovered Andean homeland.

civilizational-union.rationale: Antauro Humala envisions an Inkan International uniting Andean peoples across existing borders.

restore-past-order.rationale: Doctrine draws on Inca and Andean historical civilization as the model for Peru's foundation.

results-over-ideology.rationale: Adherents hold a distinct ideological programme and would not subordinate it to pragmatism.

direct-action.rationale: Locumba and Andahuaylas show insurgent direct action preferred to elections.

return-to-foraging.rationale: Not a position; the movement seeks a modern nation-state and national production.

abolish-division-of-labor.rationale: Not part of the programme, which is state-led national economics.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: Class dictatorship is not the doctrine; its reference group is the copper race and the nation.

collective-farming.rationale: Andean communal farming has roots, but no collectivisation programme was found.

harm-principle.rationale: Antauro Humala would limit private conduct, calling homosexuality an aberration that should stay hidden.

individual-rights-only.rationale: The doctrine assigns rights and destiny to the copper race as a group, rather than to individuals.

media-academia-power.rationale: The party proposes expropriating media outlets, implying belief that media holds undue power.

national-rebirth.rationale: Isaac Humala says Peru needs a war to awaken; the movement speaks of a national reawakening and refounding.

territorial-expansion.rationale: Isaac Humala wants Chile to return Antofagasta and territory up to the Maule; Antauro envisions a unified Andean homeland.

bound-labor.rationale: Not part of the programme; the movement claims to champion Indigenous peasants.

no-neutral-knowledge.rationale: The movement rejects Eurocentric thought and claims an Indigenous ideology, implying knowledge reflects who holds power.

jewish-state-israel.rationale: Wikipedia reports antisemitic content in the movement's newspaper; no formal position on Israel documented.

diaspora-return-right.rationale: None of the sources read mention emigrants; neutral because the doctrine gives no guidance on citizenship for Peruvians abroad.

economic-freedom.rationale: The programme subordinates the free market to national interest and would nationalise foreign firms.

rule-by-example.rationale: Adherents stress honest, heroic leadership, but no documented position on law versus example.

national-self-determination.rationale: Core demand is Indigenous Andean self-rule over a historic homeland; the movement calls itself anti-colonial.

force-without-un.rationale: Isaac Humala threatens war with Chile if the Hague ruling is not respected, implying no deference to outside bodies.

class-collaboration.rationale: Integrative nationalism uniting Peruvians under a national project is rhetorically preferred to class struggle.

dominated-front.rationale: The doctrine is anti-colonial and anti-Eurocentric and Antauro proposes an Inkan International with neighbouring Andean states.

distinct-gender-roles.rationale: Wikipedia reports machista views on women among its critics' documented charges.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: The doctrine is racialist but no segregation law is documented; it targets reversal of hierarchy, not segregation.

national-mission.rationale: The movement is inward-looking nationalism about Andean peoples, not exporting a form of government.

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: Nulled (statement review, 2026-11-11): its rationale is about elites being out of touch or general anti-establishment feeling, not about elites putting their own interests first, which this statement now asks.

reviewHistory.rationale: Isaac Humala says Peru's ruling class is detached from the country; anti-elite rhetoric is a mainstay.

night-watchman-state.rationale: The movement calls for nationalising foreign firms and a state-led economy, the opposite of a minimal state; this rests on news coverage rather than a programme text.

discourage-race-mixing.rationale: Sources conflict: CIDOB says it favours cholo and mestizo Peruvians too, while an anthropologist cited on Wikipedia says mestizos are excluded.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: The doctrine asserts the supremacy of the copper race, contradicting equal worth.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Antauro prefers strong rule and argues dictatorships have been more peaceful than democracies.

population-transfer.rationale: Wikipedia notes xenophobia toward Chile but no transfer policy.

initiating-force-wrong.rationale: Movement launched armed insurrections and its leader defends war, so adherents reject non-initiation of force.

freedom-as-non-domination.rationale: Anti-colonial themes fit, but no stated position.

vanguard-party.rationale: The Andean vanguard is military and racial, not a working-class party.

priority-to-poor.rationale: The doctrine favours Indigenous, cholo and mestizo Peruvians, who are poor.

diversity-weakens-cohesion.rationale: Ethnonationalism holds the nation is built on one people, but no direct statement on diversity.

party-controls-media.rationale: The party plans to expropriate media outlets.

representatives-worker-pay.rationale: Anti-elite rhetoric makes this plausible, but no pay policy found.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: Inkan International would pool sovereignty regionally, but adherents oppose EU-style models; split.

defeat-own-government-war.rationale: The movement is nationalist and war-affirming; undermining one's own government in war is contrary.

people-in-arms.rationale: The movement built the ASPRET militia of reservists and its uprisings were by armed supporters.

rural-life-healthier.rationale: Based in Andean Indigenous communities, which it idealises; inference only.

reunify-divided-nation.rationale: Antauro calls Peru's borders colonial impositions and envisions a unified Andean homeland.

educated-out-of-touch.rationale: Anti-elite stance; Isaac Humala calls the ruling class detached.

cultures-equal-different.rationale: The doctrine proclaims the superiority of the copper race, so adherents reject equal cultures.

sex-ed-in-schools.rationale: Hostility to homosexuality and machista views make adherents oppose such curricula.

encourage-eccentricity.rationale: Calls homosexuality a monstrosity to be kept private, favouring conformity.

independence-needs-economic-change.rationale: The programme couples national sovereignty with nationalising foreign firms and prioritising domestic production.

constituent-assembly.rationale: Antauro talks of refounding the republic; no assembly policy was confirmed.

rich-countries-aid-poor.rationale: Anti-colonial grievance might favour aid as redress, but the movement stresses national self-reliance, so adherents are plausibly split.

no-land-for-peace.rationale: Isaac Humala demands return of lost territory and rejects concessions to Chile and Bolivia.

property-serves-common-good.rationale: Nationalisation and expropriation of media subordinate private holdings to national interest.

soviet-state-capitalist.rationale: A debate among Marxists about the USSR that the Humala movement, which is racial-nationalist, has not joined.

precautionary-principle.rationale: No environmental regulatory doctrine appears in the movement's sources, so no basis for a position.

sacred-ruler.rationale: The Inca emperor was divine but adherents do not claim a divine ruler today.

character-from-environment.rationale: The doctrine attributes destiny to race, implying innate nature.

mixed-constitution.rationale: Classical theory of mixed government is not part of the doctrine, whose model is military-led nationalist rule.

leader-cult.rationale: Analysts cite fascist traits in the movement, including leader veneration.

co-ethnic-territorial-claim.rationale: Antauro claims a unified Andean homeland across current borders and rejects colonial borders.

kin-peoples-union.rationale: Nulled (statement review, 2026-11-11): its rationale is about a league, federation, cooperation or unity in general, not one state, which this statement now asks.

reviewHistory.rationale: Antauro envisions an Inkan International joining Andean peoples across borders.

national-cultural-autonomy.rationale: The movement seeks a state for the Indigenous majority, not cultural autonomy.

rights-where-you-live.rationale: The statement is about diaspora minorities and homelands; the doctrine's own claims concern an Indigenous majority at home.

material-conditions-drive-history.rationale: The doctrine is racial-nationalist rather than materialist.

economic-self-sufficiency.rationale: Priority for domestic production over imports points toward self-sufficiency.

armed-group-creates-revolution.rationale: Locumba and Andahuaylas were small armed groups trying to trigger political change.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: The doctrine aims to overturn the inherited dominance of the white elite.

history-own-civilization.rationale: The doctrine centres Inca and Indigenous civilizations and rejects Eurocentrism.

civilizing-tutelage.rationale: The movement is anti-colonial and anti-Eurocentric.

end-racial-preferences.rationale: The doctrine seeks historical redress for the copper race.

former-empire-influence.rationale: Antauro's Inkan International and Cusco-centred vision revive influence of the former Tawantinsuyo.

labor-aristocracy.rationale: A Marxist thesis about rich-country workers that this movement does not use, as it frames conflict by race and nation.

colonial-treaties-void.rationale: Antauro calls Peru's borders colonial impositions and Isaac Humala demands reversal of the Chilean settlement.

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: Locumba declared Fujimori illegitimate, showing willingness to resist a ruler seen as unlawful.

animal-suffering-matters.rationale: Animal ethics does not appear in the doctrine or its interviews, so neutral.

withdraw-from-politics.rationale: An activist insurgent movement rejects withdrawal.

return-lost-territory.rationale: Isaac Humala says Chile should return Antofagasta and land up to the Maule River and threatens war if it refuses.

indigenous-political-leadership.rationale: The doctrine asserts the supremacy of the 'copper race' as historical revenge against white-led rule.

domestic-violence-symmetry.rationale: Machista attitudes (s1) point one way, but the movement has no stated position on domestic-violence services; neutral.

institutions-fit-civilization.rationale: The movement looks to the Inca state as a model and rejects Western and colonial borders and forms of rule for Andean peoples.

military-guardian-role.rationale: The movement is military-led, founded by army officers and reservists, and acted through uprisings such as Locumba and the Andahuaylazo.

democratic-peace.rationale: Isaac Humala says war is needed to awaken the nation, which rejects the premise that democracy brings peace.

non-intervention.rationale: It seeks forceful revision of borders and claims against Chile, so it would not deny states the right to act abroad.

minority-conspiracy.rationale: The doctrine casts the white and criollo elite as the enemy of the Andean nation and seeks historical revenge on it.

abolish-legal-marriage.rationale: The movement is socially conservative and machista, with open hostility to homosexuality, so it defends traditional marriage.

informal-organisation.rationale: The movement is a military-led, hierarchical insurrectionary organisation (reservist association, Locumba, Andahuaylazo).

national-law-over-international.rationale: Its nationalism puts Peruvian sovereignty first and it rejects foreign rulings, including the Hague ruling on Chile, as Isaac Humala's interview shows.

religious-nation.rationale: The nation is defined by the copper race, not by religion, though the movement is socially conservative.

mixed-public-service-providers.rationale: Antauro Humala's proposed party would nationalise foreign companies and favour state control.

women-equality-needs-economic-change.rationale: Sources describe machista, socially conservative positions, so economic change for women is not an aim.

historical-land-claim.rationale: The movement grounds Andean Peruvians' claim to the nation in their Inca-era heritage and rejects the criollo elite's standing.

unreligious-rulers-fought.rationale: Religious law is not its standard of legitimacy; it judges rulers by national and ethnic criteria.

intersecting-oppressions.rationale: It frames oppression chiefly through race and nation, and its social positions are machista, so it rejects intersectional framing.

left-right-obsolete.rationale: The Humalas have mixed nationalism with left-leaning economics and social conservatism, but the movement does not claim to transcend left and right.

alienated-labor.rationale: A Marxist concept the movement does not use, though its state-led economics criticises market outcomes.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: Authority is grounded in the nation and race, not in God.

social-market-economy.rationale: It favours a strong state-directed, protectionist economy, which is neither laissez-faire nor exactly this mixed model; left neutral.

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: The movement is built on military reservists and insurrection and glorifies the army as the nation's instrument.

open-lgbt-military-service.rationale: Antauro Humala calls homosexuality an aberration, and the movement's military-led, machista outlook rejects open service.

abolish-police-prisons.rationale: The movement is military-led, hierarchical and built around reservists and order, so abolishing police is opposed to its core.

power-sharing-divided-societies.rationale: The doctrine asserts the leadership of the Andean 'copper race' over other Peruvians, so sharing executive power among communities contradicts it.

never-kill-self-defence.rationale: Isaac Humala says Peru needs a war and the movement staged armed insurrections, so it does not hold that killing is wrong.

unbroken-national-continuity.rationale: The movement holds that the 'copper race' continues the Inca state and takes the Inca empire as its model.

politics-spiritual-struggle.rationale: The movement is racial and military in emphasis, not spiritual; adherents are not described as holding this.

culture-before-state.rationale: The movement seeks to seize or win state power through insurrection or party politics rather than waiting for cultural renewal.

economy-in-majority-hands.rationale: The doctrine presents the copper race as the rightful core of the nation and seeks revenge on the white and criollo elite.

racial-group-interests.rationale: The doctrine centres on the copper race as the rightful core of the nation and on historical revenge against the white and criollo elite.

racial-pride.rationale: Pride in the copper race is the movement's central claim.

defensive-wars-only.rationale: Isaac Humala says Peru needs a war, and the movement demands lost territory back, so war is not limited to defence.

soldiers-refuse-war.rationale: The movement glorifies war and military action, including a desired war with Chile, so refusing to fight is the opposite of its stance.

in-work-tax-credits.rationale: Never addressed; adherents' state-led economics would allow it but the movement states no view.

smash-state-machine.rationale: The movement sought power by armed uprising against the existing government, though its aim was a new nationalist state rather than abolition of the state.

sacred-nation.rationale: The movement presents the 'copper race' and the Peruvian nation as the central community, with the Inca state as its ideal.

internal-colonialism.rationale: The movement frames Andean Peru as dominated and exploited by the white and criollo coastal elite.

shared-human-nature.rationale: The movement ranks peoples by race, so it does not rest dignity on a single shared human nature.

women-property-inheritance.rationale: Adherents are machista and socially conservative, but the movement also honours Andean communal tradition; no stated position.

democracy-is-procedure.rationale: Antauro Humala has said that dictatorship can be acceptable, and the movement pursued insurrection and military rule rather than electoral competition.

race-social-construct.rationale: The doctrine of the 'copper race' treats race as a real basis of national identity and historical revenge.

keep-colonial-borders.rationale: Isaac Humala demands Chile return Antofagasta and land to the Maule River, and the movement contests colonial-era divisions through its 'Inkan International' idea.

homeland-spiritual-bond.rationale: Nulled (statement review, 2026-11-11): its rationale is about defending or claiming the homeland, not a spiritual bond with it, which is all the statement now asks about.

reviewHistory.rationale: The movement presents the Andean 'copper race' as rightful heir to the Inca homeland and demands recovery of lost territory.
reviewHistory.author: claude-sonnet-5-5

reviewHistory.rationale: Nulled (statement review, 2026-11-11): its rationale is about defending or claiming the homeland, not a spiritual bond with it, which is all the statement now asks about.
reviewHistory.author: claude-opus-5-5

wife-divorce-without-consent.rationale: Reported machista, socially conservative positions, including Antauro's condemnation of homosexuality and civil unions.

national-resource-control.rationale: The movement's proposals include nationalising foreign companies and putting domestic production first.

racism-not-main-obstacle.rationale: The movement is built on the claim that Peru's racial hierarchy still subordinates the copper race to the white elite.

patriotism-serves-workers.rationale: Its nationalism is joined to a state-led economy meant to serve the Andean majority, as the summary of sources describes.

material-over-identity.rationale: Race and ethnic identity are the core of the doctrine, so it puts them ahead of material interests.

former-empire-equal-treatment.rationale: Antauro's Inkan International and Cusco-centred vision revive influence of the former Tawantinsuyo. (Carried over from former-empire-influence, "A country should cultivate political and cultural influence in regions once ruled by its predecessor empire.", with the value reversed, 2026-11-11.)

missingStatements.text: A country should demand the return of territory it lost to a neighbour in a past war.
missingStatements.rationale: Isaac Humala says Chile should return Antofagasta and land up to the Maule River and threatens war if it refuses.

missingStatements.text: The descendants of a country's pre-colonial peoples should hold political leadership over the descendants of settlers.
missingStatements.rationale: The doctrine asserts the supremacy of the 'copper race' as historical revenge against white-led rule.

notes: Sources on the doctrine are mostly critical or journalistic; the movement's Ideario was not accessible. Ollanta Humala's integrative nationalism would answer many identity and economic items far more moderately. Sources disagree on whether mestizos are included in the 'copper race'.
